item.title: Onboard your AI agents like new hires to prevent automated mistakes
item.description:
Imagine a brand-new marketing hire being handed a spreadsheet and expected to execute a campaign on day one. Would you blame them if it went badly, when no one had explained customer profiles, conversion goals, or lead qualification criteria?

AI agents may be the largest batch of new hires your company will bring on for years to come. Like any new employee, they start without the institutional knowledge their experienced colleagues have acquired on the job. They aren’t familiar with your data assets, your company goals, or the semantics that make your business unique.

Give an agent raw data without that context, and it will behave like a poorly trained employee, misinterpreting goals and concepts while bypassing required procedures. This is the context ceiling most enterprise AI pilots hit long before model intelligence becomes a limiting factor.

How you onboard agents, and the context you feed them, will determine whether they become productive members of the enterprise or merely automate mistakes at great speed.

Move beyond traditional data catalogs to onboard AI agents effectively

For many enterprises, the obvious place to start onboarding agents is their existing data catalog. Give an agent access to the company’s data and definitions, and it should have what it needs to get to work. The problem is that traditional catalogs were designed for human discovery, not the constantly changing, task-specific context that agents require. Much of that knowledge also lives elsewhere, spread across process documents, chat histories, data systems, and the accumulated know-how of experienced employees.

We’re moving from cataloging everything and searching it later to assembling context around intent.

Agents need context organized around the job they’re asked to do. If an agent is running a marketing campaign, it shouldn’t have to sift through everything the company knows to find what matters. A context layer can start with the marketing task, pull in the relevant institutional knowledge, and serve the agent only what it needs. It then has to keep learning, as definitions, processes, and business conditions change. Agents can help prune stale information and flag conflicting definitions, with people reviewing the cases that require judgment.

Treat AI context like code to keep it versioned, open, and governed

An enterprise context layer goes beyond documenting what data exists and what it means. It organizes the data, business semantics, processes, and institutional knowledge around the agent’s intent. That context may be structured or unstructured and distributed across cloud and on-premises systems.

To keep that context from scattering across teams and systems, leaders should connect these assets into a dynamic context graph that self-learns from different organizational signals. Code repositories, data assets, tribal knowledge sources such as chat threads and meeting notes, user roles, and organizational structure all provide context about how the business operates and how its entities relate to one another.

Context changes constantly as business definitions evolve and trusted sources go stale. Treating context like code means tracking versions, keeping an audit trail, and being able to roll back changes. Teams should also be able to export part of the context layer, experiment with it outside the main branch, and merge it back.

CIOs need visibility into what context is stored, how it’s used, and the identity an agent is operating under. When an agent acts on someone’s behalf, it should only see what that person is authorized to see. Autonomous agents should operate under their own identities with independently granted permissions.

For critical business metrics, verified SQL patterns known as golden queries can give agents a trusted path to the answer without asking the model to calculate it from scratch. Open standards such as the Open Knowledge Format can keep context portable as companies adopt new models and agent tools. Those technologies will change. The proprietary knowledge that teaches them how your business works is far more durable.

As enterprises move from deploying a handful of agents to potentially millions, context becomes an infrastructure problem. CIOs need a shared context layer with enterprise-grade security, scalability, and availability. Without one, context can sprawl across agents and applications, creating new silos of organizational knowledge that become increasingly difficult to govern and keep consistent.

Capture institutional knowledge to build a competitive AI moat

Frontier models arrive knowing very little about how a particular business works. Your data, definitions, processes, and operational know-how fill that gap. Capture that knowledge as reusable context, and the next agent you deploy can benefit from what the organization has already learned.

Capturing context is only useful if an agent can find the right piece when it needs it. Context retrieval should factor in the task, the role of the agent, and the operating environment to deliver the optimal slice of context, enabling agents to generate insights and take action efficiently. This helps cut unnecessary tokens and tool calls while improving the speed, relevance, and accuracy of responses.

Models and agent tools will come and go. The institutional knowledge used to onboard them can get richer with every agent you deploy, becoming an asset competitors can’t buy or replicate.

item.title: Secure your AI estate: 5 things CIOs must know about AI agents
item.description:
What CIOs need to know about AI agents

Enterprise AI adoption is entering a new phase. Generative AI gave employees new ways to create content and access information, primarily through AI web applications. Embedded AI copilots began helping them work natively in existing applications.

Now, AI agents are running locally on employee workstations, with expansive user permissions, and are increasingly capable of autonomously executing work.

An AI agent is an LLM-powered software system that can reason over context, make decisions, and pursue an objective with a degree of autonomy. Unlike conventional software built around predefined logic, agents introduce probabilistic, context-sensitive reasoning into how tasks are interpreted and executed. They can interpret changing inputs, determine what to do next, use tools and enterprise systems, and adapt as a task unfolds.

The progression from answers to actions has significant implications for CIOs. Here are five things technology leaders must understand as powerful endpoint agents like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex become part of everyday enterprise operations.

1. AI is evolving from answering questions to executing work

The simplest way to understand AI agents is to look at how enterprise AI has evolved.

A chatbot answers a question. A copilot works alongside a person in an existing workflow, where it helps draft content or analyze information. An endpoint AI agent goes further: A person provides the objective; the agent determines the steps required to accomplish it.

That distinction matters. An endpoint agent may gather information, break a goal into tasks, choose among available tools, complete steps, and adjust as conditions change. Instead of helping a human perform a workflow, the agent can autonomously create and execute its own workflow without waiting for human direction.

For CIOs, this makes agentic AI more than a productivity feature. As AI moves from generating content to executing work, it changes the role software can play throughout the enterprise.

2. Agents combine reasoning with the authority to act

Agents become consequential when reasoning is combined with enterprise authority.

They can interpret a goal, plan how to accomplish it, and interact with APIs, applications, databases, development environments, files, or other services. They execute tasks using the access and capabilities available to the user, service, or identity they operate on behalf of.

Consider a developer asking an agent to troubleshoot a deployment. The agent might inspect source code, search documentation, query a cloud environment, run a command, modify a file, and validate whether the change worked. What began as one human instruction can become a sequence of actions across several systems, all conducted with the developer’s level of access.

This is the fundamental shift CIOs need to account for. The question is no longer simply what an AI system can tell an employee. It is increasingly what the AI system can do on the organization’s behalf. AI agents can become the insider threat that you never onboarded.

3. Agents operate at machine scale

Human interaction with AI is constrained by human speed and bandwidth. People type prompts, review responses, make decisions, and initiate next steps sequentially, as humans cannot execute tasks in parallel.

Agents move at machine speed. They can spin up sub-agents and execute a huge volume of tasks in parallel, at unprecedented scale. CrowdStrike internal usage data found that endpoint AI agents consumed roughly 700 times more tokens than humans using AI chatbots via the browser.

The significance is not token consumption alone. As organizations deploy more agents, they create dramatically more AI activity and telemetry to capture, understand, store, and correlate.

This creates an operational challenge. Architectures and governance models designed around human-paced interaction may struggle when thousands of software actors begin operating simultaneously at machine speed.

4. Agentic misalignment can cause breaches

An AI agent does not have to be compromised to create risk. It can pursue a legitimate objective in an unsafe or unexpected way, especially when it has broad access to enterprise systems and is operating without continuous human direction.

For example, an agent tasked with sharing information could decide that uploading a file to a public file-sharing service is the fastest way to complete the job, even if the file contains sensitive corporate data. The agent may be accomplishing the objective it was given, but not in a way the organization intended. As agents take more autonomous action, their activity is becoming increasingly material to security teams.

According to the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report, CrowdStrike is seeing AI agent-triggered detection leads at 2.5 times the rate of human-triggered leads.

This doesn’t mean agents are inherently malicious. It illustrates how quickly autonomous systems can generate security-relevant activity when they can act continuously through enterprise identities and permissions.

For CIOs, this creates practical questions: Who owns each agent? What is it supposed to do? What systems can it access? Under whose authority does it operate? What activity should require human approval? When its behavior moves outside intended boundaries, who is responsible for intervening?

Organizations already have mature processes for onboarding employees and managing applications. Agents increasingly require the same level of operational accountability.

5. Agents connect enterprise technology layers

Most technology shifts created a distinct domain that CIOs learned to manage: endpoints, networks, cloud infrastructure, SaaS applications, identity systems, and data platforms.

Agents are different because they can operate across all of them at once. CrowdStrike describes this interconnected environment as the AI estate, which spans data, models, prompts, agents, identities, infrastructure, and interactions.

CIOs need visibility into what agents exist, as well as their ownership and purpose, appropriate access, runtime behavior, and clear boundaries for when humans remain in control. The goal is to create the operating model that allows organizations to scale it safely.

item.title: ServiceNow makes it easier to build AI agents, gives them verifiable identities
item.description:
ServiceNow is giving its AI Control Tower new features to make AI agents more governable — and a new name, Super Intelligence Control Tower (SICT), to please the US President. It is also updating EmployeeWorks to make building AI agents easier.

AI Passport, a new component of SICT, gives every agent, whether from ServiceNow or a third party, a verifiable identity, and provides runtime control over its activities.

As enterprises scale autonomous agents from pilots to production, they are facing new challenges, said Nenshad Bardoliwalla, SVP of AI product management at ServiceNow: “If companies can’t identify which agents are running, what they are doing, and what systems they can access, then scaling quickly becomes a risk.”

An AI Passport is a cryptographically signed credential for AI agents that is checked at runtime to verify the scope authorized by the enterprise. When an AI agent stays within its passport scope, it can operate freely, but if it tries to deviate, defined actions are enforced. These can include redirecting, restricting, or reconnecting the agent with proper context, or even triggering a kill switch. All actions are audited so agent activity can be tracked.

It is built on open specifications, so any governance product, identity provider, or enforcement point can issue and verify credentials for their own and third-party AI agents, and those credentials are verifiable at every step in multi-agent workflows.

A bouncer at every door

This is a real step forward, said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research. “Most agent governance today is a security camera. It records what happened so someone can review the tape later. AI Passport is a bouncer at every door.”

The controls extend beyond ServiceNow’s own agents, he said: “For third-party agents, the passport replaces the agent’s own ‘claims’ about its permissions,” he said. “Taking an agent’s word for what it is allowed to do is an Achilles’ heel of agentic AI.”

And, he said, “A passport is only as trustworthy as the office that issues it. Here, the issuing office is ServiceNow’s CMDB, its GRC policies, and its workflow approvals. If that data is stale, the passport is stale. Credit ServiceNow for building on open specifications, but an open spec matters only when others adopt it. Nvidia is the launch partner, and ServiceNow says that enforcement implementation is still being built.”

In addition to AI Passport, ServiceNow has further beefed up its governance tools with a number of other features, including shadow-AI detection to locate unapproved agents on the network; more than 400 connectors to enable AI discovery across platforms and vendors; access mapping; and continuous enterprise AI observability.

It also announced cost governance; “value intelligence” that connects consumption, cost, quality, and “realized user value” to help teams optimize their AI use; AI cost management as part of ServiceNow IT Asset Management, which integrates with the Control Tower; and policy enforcement.

AI Passport, Shadow AI detection, and AI Cost Management are expected to be available by year end.

EmployeeWorks enhancements

The third generation of ServiceNow EmployeeWorks now lets employees add automations to the autonomous AI personal assistants they build. ToolSmith is a new agentic developer environment that takes tool building “from days to minutes,” the company said.

What companies have been trying to do, said Bhavin Shah, SVP of ServiceNow’s employee experience group, “is to give developers a way to build, but in a way that’s governed, that allows them to stay within the guardrails and the controls that that are required in order to do the kinds of safe but deep and capable work that they want for their constituents inside the company.”

ToolSmith helps address that problem. It’s a vibe-coding environment with which developers can build automations for ServiceNow EmployeeWorks AI assistants by describing what they need in natural language. ServiceNow said ToolSmith was trained on over 75,000 APIs and optimized for reliability and token efficiency. Developers can test and refine its output using the same conversational interface.

ServiceNow said that ToolSmith also identifies what to build next, scanning logs “to identify opportunities to fix, improve, or invent the next best workflow.”

Non-coding employees, on the other hand, can build new Productivity Assistants to perform contextual or persona-based work including long-running tasks, the company said. There are also pre-built assistants available, beginning with several for HR service delivery.

EmployeeWorks itself includes two assistants out of the box: a research assistant that can scan internal and external sources for answers, based on the user’s role, and a calendaring assistant that, ServiceNow said, “goes beyond typical calendar booking solutions by orchestrating nuanced requests like scheduling quarterly one-on-ones with an entire team on days that minimize disruption to project work or finding the least hectic day to bring together a team for a full day workshop. “

To automate repetitive tasks, Productivity Routines run proactively in the background, repeating routine steps and providing deliverables without human intervention. Employees just have to describe what they want to automate, select the necessary tools, and deploy the routine.

“The principle is right,” Dickson said. “The people closest to the work understand the problem best.”

But, he added, “the guardrails are only as good as the decisions behind them. Productivity Routines, by ServiceNow’s description, run in the background without human intervention. That is unsupervised work, and someone should own it.”

All of these EmployeeWorks enhancements are in controlled availability now.

Bottom line

Melody Brue, analyst in residence at Moor Insights & Strategy, said the announcements are a sign that ServiceNow is extending its existing security and workflow controls into a broader role in governing agent actions across systems.

“AI Passport makes identity and authorized scope verifiable, Control Tower provides oversight and enforcement, and ToolSmith expands the tools and connectors through which agents can act within enterprise guardrails,” she said, adding that with CEO Bill McDermott’s recent positioning of ServiceNow as a security company, “This suggests an ambition to become a control point for enterprise autonomy.”

But, she said, “What matters now is how consistently ServiceNow can enforce boundaries and verify outcomes across the systems agents actually touch.”

Dickson, too, has concerns.

“ServiceNow says Control Tower tracks spending by user, department, and runtime, and ties that spend to quality and value. The brake is another matter,” he noted. “The graduated alert, throttle, and block enforcement is described in future tense, as is the AI Cost Management integration, which is expected by year end.”

However, “a meter you can watch is not a brake,” he said. “A Productivity Routine that runs every morning is a standing purchase order. Someone should sign it.”

Give every agent and every routine a named owner and a budget before it goes live, he advised, and ask ServiceNow how assists are counted for background routines and whether hard caps exist today. Turn on throttling the day it ships, and reconcile its dashboards against your own invoices.

But despite these concerns, he said, ServiceNow has the right idea. “An agent should carry its permissions, its manager, and its budget wherever it goes. But until the brakes ship, that budget is a decision a person still has to make.”

item.title: What a cockatoo can teach us about the evidence AI wasn’t built to hear
item.description:
AI systems do not make decisions from reality. They make decisions from representations of reality: records, observations, measurements, histories, labels, documents, and whatever else an organization has decided belongs in the data. That distinction sounds almost too obvious to be interesting, yet it becomes surprisingly easy to forget once an AI system can process thousands of records, identify patterns no person would notice, and return an answer that appears comprehensive. The sophistication of the analysis can distract us from a more basic problem: important information may never enter the decision process in a form the system can use.

Much of the responsible-AI conversation begins after that problem has already occurred. We ask whether a model is accurate, whether its recommendation can be explained, whether a human remains involved, and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Those are necessary questions, but they assume that the relevant evidence made it into the decision somewhere. If the AI and the human reviewer are both reasoning from the same incomplete representation, adding a person at the end does not necessarily repair what was missing at the beginning. I spend a great deal of time thinking about consequential AI decisions and the conditions organizations need in order to govern them responsibly, but what made me look at this particular problem differently was not another governance framework or model-risk paper. It was a small white parrot named Ellie.

Ellie is a Goffin’s cockatoo, a species known for sophisticated problem-solving. She has participated in a multiyear animal-computer interaction research program led by Jennifer Taylor-O’Connor, who previously published as Jennifer Cunha, and researchers from several universities. The work examines what happens when parrots are given access to tablets, speech boards, video communication, and other technologies that let researchers systematically observe their choices and behavior. The important part of this research is not the internet-friendly question of whether a bird can “talk” or “read.” The progression of the research is more useful than that because the questions become progressively more demanding.

A 2024 CHI paper, Ellie Talks About the Weather, examined the expressive and enrichment potential of a tablet-based speech board used by a single Goffin’s cockatoo. The work was not presented as proof that parrots possess human language; it examined the interaction itself and what could reasonably be inferred from it.

Later that year, Communication Functions in Speech Board Use by a Goffin’s Cockatoo examined Ellie’s speech-board behavior against recognized functions of communication. The researchers examined her persistence when requests were not fulfilled, her ability to locate displaced representations of preferred items, and her responses when she received something different from what she selected. The authors concluded that the combined findings aligned with recognized linguistic and biological communication functions and indicated intentional communication. The paper received an Honorable Mention Award at the 2024 International Conference on Animal-Computer Interaction.

The research has since moved into territory that should feel familiar to anyone designing or governing AI systems. A 2026 CHI study involving Taylor-O’Connor examines how different speech-board representations affect parrots’ selections. Humans determine which options are available, how those options are represented, what counts as a selection, what is recorded, and how the resulting behavior is interpreted. The signal does not arrive untouched; the interface shapes what becomes observable evidence.

Ellie may be exceptional. Her abilities, training history, environment, and years of interaction with these systems do not make her representative of cockatoos generally, much less animals as a whole. I do not think she needs to be representative for the case to matter. Edge cases are often useful because they expose assumptions that ordinary cases leave hidden. Ellie does not prove that animals generally can communicate through technology in the same way. She shows that changing the interface can change what information becomes available to us. For anyone responsible for enterprise AI, that should feel familiar, because organizations constantly decide not only what information is true or reliable, but what information can enter a system at all.

The record is not the subject

Organizations routinely translate complicated lives and situations into forms they can process. A patient becomes diagnoses, medications, laboratory values, codes, and clinical notes. An employee becomes performance measures, tickets, evaluations, attendance, and productivity data. An applicant becomes income, history, scores, documents, and eligibility fields. An animal in a veterinary or shelter environment becomes medical history, behavioral observations, intake information, caregiver notes, and disposition status. We cannot avoid representation; no human decision-maker or AI system can absorb reality in its entirety. The problem begins when the representation starts functioning as though it were sufficient for the reality it describes.

Consider an AI-assisted system supporting a consequential animal-care decision involving treatment, rehabilitation, social placement, or transfer to another facility. The system has medical information, behavioral observations, caregiver notes, placement history, environmental factors, and perhaps outcomes from similar cases. It analyzes those inputs and recommends a course of action. A veterinarian or experienced animal-care professional reviews the recommendation and retains final authority. Nothing about that arrangement sounds obviously irresponsible. Human judgment remains in the process, and the AI supports rather than makes the final decision.

Now suppose another source of information exists that does not fit comfortably into the established record. Repeated observations may indicate a social attachment that matters to the proposed placement. The animal may consistently avoid an environment that appears suitable on paper. In some future setting, a sufficiently validated communication interface may provide additional information about preference, discomfort, social interaction, or another state relevant to the decision. None of that should automatically override clinical judgment or an AI-supported recommendation. Animal-generated signals can be ambiguous, interfaces can shape responses, and welfare needs can conflict with preference. What matters is whether the decision process has a legitimate way to receive and consider that information once it becomes credible enough to matter.

The same problem exists in human settings, although it is easier to overlook because we tend to assume people can correct the record themselves. A patient can explain that symptoms have changed, an employee can challenge an evaluation, an applicant can provide additional circumstances, or someone denied a service can appeal. In practice, those pathways are uneven. Disability, language, age, institutional power, rigid forms, inaccessible processes, and simply not knowing what a system has inferred can all affect whether someone can put missing context back into a decision. Ellie makes the structural assumption easier to see because she cannot compensate for a poorly designed channel in the ways our institutions expect humans to. If an interface gives her no way to express something, she cannot add a note explaining what is missing. If humans misinterpret her behavior, she cannot request a meeting to clarify what she meant. Researchers therefore have to confront the channel’s design rather than assume the subject will repair whatever the system failed to capture.

The problem starts before the model does

This is where the issue becomes particularly relevant to CIOs and enterprise technology leaders. We often talk about an AI model as though it independently determines which information matters. In reality, many of those decisions are made long before inference begins. Someone decided what fields would exist, what could be measured, whose observations would be recorded, which systems would exchange information, what metadata would survive transformation, and which sources the model would be allowed to retrieve. By the time the AI appears, a large part of the evidence environment has already been designed.

That is why I do not think this is simply a conventional data-quality problem. A record can be accurate and still be incomplete. Every field can be populated correctly while the system remains incapable of receiving another category of information that could materially affect the decision. A medical intake system can add dozens of fields and still fail to capture an experience the form was never designed to describe. A workforce platform can generate increasingly detailed performance metrics while measuring only the work that is easy to quantify. An animal communication interface can record every available selection perfectly while still limiting the subject to choices humans decided to make available.

The 2026 parrot-interface research makes that mediation unusually obvious. The interface is not a transparent pipe carrying an untouched preference from animal to researcher. It is part of the process through which something becomes interpretable evidence. Enterprise systems work the same way, although the mediation is usually hidden inside familiar databases, APIs, forms, workflow rules, scoring systems, and integration decisions. Those systems do not merely store information; they define the channels through which information becomes visible and actionable.

For CIOs, that creates a question upstream of model selection and model evaluation. When designing an AI system for a consequential workflow, someone should ask not only whether the data is accurate, governed, secure, and traceable, but what materially relevant evidence has no pathway into the system at all. A high-performing model cannot compensate for information the surrounding architecture cannot receive, and human review does not automatically solve the problem if the reviewer is constrained by the same representation.

That raises an obvious challenge: how would an organization ever know whether it has enough information? In most consequential decisions, it probably cannot know that the picture is complete. Complete information is not a realistic governance standard. Decisions are made under uncertainty all the time, and waiting for perfect knowledge can itself create harm. Organizations can become much more explicit about decision sufficiency: whether the available evidence is adequate for the consequence at stake, what meaningful uncertainty remains, and what kinds of new information would be important enough to reopen the decision.

That distinction matters because sufficiency should be proportional to consequence. The evidence required to recommend a playlist should not resemble the evidence expected before denying medical treatment, terminating employment, transferring a vulnerable animal, or making a high-consequence public-sector decision. As consequences become more serious, harder to reverse, or more dependent on assumptions about an affected subject, the case for actively looking for missing evidence becomes stronger. The organization does not need omniscience, but it should be able to explain why the available information was considered adequate and what would have changed that judgment.

In practice, that means asking questions that sit slightly outside traditional model evaluation. What evidence, if it existed, could materially change this recommendation? Which perspectives or sources are missing from the current record? Are there known channels through which contradictory or contextual information can enter the workflow? What assumptions are being made because certain information is unavailable? How reversible is the decision if those assumptions prove wrong? Answers will vary by domain, but the discipline of asking them shifts the standard from “the model had enough data to run” to “the organization had enough evidence to justify acting.”

This is where the governance conversation becomes more useful. Model performance can tell us whether an AI system performs well against the information it receives. It cannot tell us whether the evidence environment itself was sufficient for the decision. That question belongs partly to data architecture, partly to workflow design, partly to governance, and partly to the domain professionals who understand what the record may be leaving out.

A second mirror

Something else about Ellie’s research has stayed with me because it creates an unusual contrast with the way we talk about AI. We are building artificial systems whose language is so fluent that people routinely have to be reminded not to confuse convincing output with understanding. We worry, appropriately, about assigning too much intelligence, intention, confidence, or authority to a machine because it communicates in a form humans find natural.

At the same time, researchers are developing technologies that may allow us to perceive forms of animal communication that humans have historically struggled to recognize. There, the error can run in the opposite direction. Scientific caution about anthropomorphism is essential, but unfamiliar communication can also be discounted because it does not arrive in a form our institutions naturally recognize as evidence. The useful comparison is not whether AI and animals “really understand” in some equivalent sense. They are not equivalent, and forcing the discussion there would turn a governance problem into a philosophical argument it does not need. What connects them is human judgment. We decide when a signal appears meaningful, which sources deserve credibility, what becomes part of a record, and how much weight different forms of evidence receive.

Once those judgments are encoded into enterprise systems, AI can reproduce them with tremendous consistency. That consistency is useful when the underlying assumptions are sound, but much less reassuring when they are not. A system can appear technically sophisticated while remaining blind to information that never fit the architecture. In that sense, Ellie’s value to this conversation is not that she tells us something universal about animal intelligence. She makes one hidden assumption visible: changing the channel can change what information becomes available, and information that cannot enter a system cannot influence the decision no matter how sophisticated the analysis becomes.

As AI moves deeper into healthcare, employment, financial services, public services, animal care, and other consequential environments, we will continue improving model evaluation, explainability, human oversight, contestability, accountability, and data governance. We should. But those safeguards begin too late if the evidence architecture around the decision was insufficient from the start.

The practical standard is not that organizations must somehow know everything before an AI-supported decision can proceed. That would be impossible. The more defensible standard is that they should know why they believe they have enough, what uncertainty they are accepting, and what new evidence would require them to reconsider. Sometimes the model will process the available record correctly, the human reviewer will do exactly what policy requires, and every formal control will operate as designed. The decision may still rest on an incomplete picture, but an organization that has explicitly considered evidentiary sufficiency is in a very different position from one that simply assumed the record was the whole story.

That may be the quieter governance lesson hiding inside an unusual cockatoo experiment. Better AI will help us extract more meaning from the information we already possess. Responsible AI also requires enough humility to ask what the system was never designed to receive—and whether that missing piece is important enough that we should go looking for it before we act.

item.title: How to make sense of the agentic AI tools ecosystem
item.description:
For the past half century or more, the teams running enterprise software stacks have nurtured a vast ecosystem of tools to keep software humming along. They’ve built CI/CD pipelines, elaborate test suites, code repositories, and tools galore, all with the goal of keeping the systems up and running.

Now AI is throwing a wrench into the whole endeavor. Software is now more complex and sometimes mysteriously unpredictable. Expectations are sky high, but no one is certain what to expect in good conscience.

Luckily, dozens of companies are rushing to build new tools designed to keep agentic stacks on the straight and narrow, delivering value to everyone. The field is rapidly evolving, probably having changed since you started reading this article.

Some of the tools involved in the emerging agent stack aren’t that different from what enterprise teams already have in store. In the end, LLMs are just piles of bits that need to be loaded into a processing chip, just like old-fashioned software. Many of the old tools that watch for overloaded nodes or overpacked disk drives are just as valuable as ever, perhaps more so because LLMs chew through storage even faster. And some of the companies tackling these problems are the same steadfast suppliers who have earned the trust of your DevOps teams; they’ve just extended their own offerings to handle LLMs and AI.

Other challenges, however, are quite different. For example, LLMs are terrifyingly non-deterministic, a real challenge for belts-and-suspenders engineers who traditionally tend the software. Tool vendors are building entirely new systems to handle these somewhat random deviations so that traditional DevOps teams — and their C-suites — don’t have heart attacks.

The field is also rapidly expanding in wildly divergent ways. Some vendors are building tools for developers who are creating new LLMs. Others are concentrating on the challenges that come from worrying about an LLM, day in and day out, in large scale production.

We’ve compiled lists introducing the most intriguing companies developing tools for this rapidly altering space, including tools aimed at AI orchestration; AI observability, aka AgentOps; AI evaluation and benchmarking; and AI trust, guardrail, and governance. We’ve even thrown in some vibe-coding tools for citizen development and AI workflow tools for business processes.

While it was relatively easy to split the field into distinct lists, that process will only grow more challenging because the tools — and categories — are starting to overlap. As vendors evolve their strategies, this overlap will grow further, with a variety of entries tackling a wider range of challenges, vying for a greater percentage of CIOs’ AI middleware and operational budgets.

To help you make sense of this complex tool landscape, here are the most common categories vendors are using to identify what their products do, each of which maps to what are becoming the key components IT needs to keep their AI and agentic stacks productive and humming.

Tools for Your AI Fleet

• 16 governance tools for securing your AI fleet

• 20 AI workflow tools for adding intelligence to business processes

• 21 agent orchestration tools for managing your AI fleet

• 19 AgentOps tools for monitoring AI activity, issues, and costs

• 13 tools for evaluating and benchmarking agentic AI systems

• 19 vibe coding tools for democratizing app development

Observability

Vendors often use the term “observability” to refer to the most basic of data collection work — that is, testing to make sure the various machines are running, the RAM isn’t too full, latency is acceptable, and the logs aren’t filled with error codes.

Watching these metrics isn’t much different from caring for an old-school collection of microservices, and often the tools aren’t much different, either. Many of the most popular tools are the same dominant market leaders that have been extended to collect data from the various GPUs, too.

Leading vendors: DataDog, Dynatrace, New Relic, Splunk
Upstarts: Ariz, LangSmith, Braintrust, Galileo
Open-source alternatives: OpenTelemetry, Phoenix, Langfuse

Cost engineering

Many AI pipelines are often more complex than regular microservice architectures, and that means they need someone to carefully watch the bill. Plus, as attention to AI ROI rises, capturing spend is essential — especially given how quickly AI tokens can add up.

Cost engineering tools can integrate information from various portals like OpenRouter and compare it against internal hardware. Sometimes breaking down these comparisons is difficult because the right way to allocate costs to each user isn’t as obvious, even though they’re often just one number. These accounting operations tools will become even more important as LLM bills grow.

Leading vendors: CloudZero, Finout
Upstarts:  Amnic, Bifrost, Portkey
Open-source alternatives: OpenCost, Langfuse

AgentOps

When metrics and telemetry begin to focus on the LLM, the word “AgentOps” starts to appear. It’s just like DevOps but it’s concerned with watching token counts, tracking the performance of RAG databases, and collecting traces for debugging purposes.

When the work is truly agentic, AgentOps must also juggle the state that agents generate while looping through their various activities. Agents aren’t just a one-and-done call to an LLM. They’re software packages that need to store information as they work toward a final answer.

This job of an AgentsOps team gets trickier because these areas are where the models often behave non-deterministically. Is some model hallucinating? Are an agent’s prompt chains running to completion? The tools in this space track all these metrics, often in a dashboard with nice graphs that make problems stand out.

Leading vendors: Databricks, Datadog, Dynatrace
Upstarts: Arize, Braintrust, Comet
Open-source alternatives: Langfus, LlamaIndex

Evaluation

The buzzword “evaluation” starts to appear alongside tools that are used in the earlier stages of development, when various models and prompt combinations need to be tested again and again.

In many cases, these tools use another model to evaluate the quality of the answer from the first model, as well as to keep an eye out for potential hallucinations or other failures. In some cases, the tools query humans who sit in the evaluation loop to give their opinions of how well the model is performing. Good tools can watch the agents continuously and reroute any sketchy behavior to the human-in-the-loop.

Many of the vendors use the word “evaluation” to describe measuring just how well a model is performing for a particular business application. That is, how well it’s working for what your boss wants it to do.

Leading vendors: Databricks, SuperAnnotate, Scale AI
Upstarts: Braintrust, Galileo AI, MaximAI
Open-source alternatives: Langfuse, Prompfoo, Tagas

Benchmarking

The word “benchmarking” is similar to “evaluation” in AI vendor literature, but it is usually found more in the tools used by the creators of the models. There are a number of public benchmarks filled with standard queries, and the model developers rank themselves on how well they do solving these problems. This often generates a raw score that is then compared to another’s raw number. Some teams create their own benchmarking problem sets and use them during evaluation to assess how well models might meet their needs.

Leading vendors: Hugging Face, Databricks
Upstarts: Reka AI, Patronus AI
Open-source alternatives: Promptfoo, DeepEval

Trust

The tools that wear the “trust” benchmark are often meant to help evaluate how well a model is protecting the needs of any business that is deploying it. That is, can they trust it to deliver accurate and useful answers without hallucinations, data leakage, inappropriate behavior, or worse? Prompts with malicious instructions are especially tricky to detect. Some enterprises want a trust score that measures the consistency of the answers. Overall, tools that target the “trust” metric are often utilized more during development and early deployment.

Leading vendors: Azure AI Content Safety, Bedrock Guardrails, Vertex AI Search
Upstarts: Patronus AI, Arthur AI
Open-source alternatives: NeMo Guardrails, Llama Guard

Guardrails

The word “guardrails” is usually applied to tools that are part of the deployment stack. That is, they sit as watchdogs and make sure the LLM doesn’t spin out of control. They also ensure the model is trustworthy, but they’re more tuned to operating in real-time than those aimed at trust, as outlined above.

These tools are often filled with fixed rules, such as scanning for social security numbers or watching for noxious words. The challenges get trickier because agents are executing software, and that means the guardrails must do more than analyze outputs. They also need to manage the execution environment, often running in a sandbox, and watch for exploits and other malicious behavior. They need to validate and double-check not just code, but the OS-level commands for manipulating files and processes.

Leading vendors: Azure AI Content Safety, Bedrock Guardrails, Vertex AI Search
Upstarts: Patronus AI, Arthur AI
Open-source alternatives: NeMo Guardrails, Llama Guard

Context

Many systems rely on a vector database to store embedded data to chunks of trustworthy documents. These RAG databases need much of the same care as regular databases, and the tools for their care are often similar. PostgreSQL, for example, has a vector addition that needs the same kind of scrutiny from a database administrator as a regular PostgreSQL database.

Leading vendors: MongoDB, Elasticsearch
Upstarts: Pinecone, Weaviate
Open-source alternatives: Milvus, PostgreSQL

Gateway routing

Increasingly, AI systems employ models in constellations, and a gateway router is what examines a prompt to determine which model or agent is best for answering the query. Moreover, as agents undertake their work, the router can distribute the agent’s various subcalls to the fastest, cheapest, or most accurate LLM or subagent.

Watching over this stage in the pipeline requires a different set of intelligence because the questions can often involve both applicability and cost. Sometimes this layer must balance the extra cost versus the need for a better answer.

Leading vendors: Cloudflare, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure
Upstarts: OpenRouter, ModelsLab, Respan
Open-source alternatives: LangChain, Bifrost, LiteLLM

Access control

Who gets to use the model? Who is paying? Many access control tools are the same ones that were part of standard APIs or web services. Is there an API key? Is the account below its budget? The tools watch for overspending because both the customer and the boss want to make sure the money keeps flowing and no tokens are wasted.

Leading vendors: Auth0, Apigee
Upstarts: Amnic, Portfoundry
Open-source alternatives: LiteLLM, Bifrost

Compliance

Some industries have explicit compliance requirements dictated by law. Some have their own internal controls. Tools devoted to compliance are often a subset of the ones devoted to guardrails. But they’re often treated separately from guardrail tools because they’re more likely to be of interest to lawyers and that makes the stakes higher.

Leading vendors: ServiceNow, IBM
Upstarts: VerifyWise, Norm AI
Open-source alternatives: Aether, Giskard

item.title: Token efficiency: Building AI that spends intelligence wisely
item.description:
Last year, my company decided to rebuild our enterprise AI platform, which our customers had been using for over a decade. But instead of simply updating it, we started over with a different ambition: to build an AI-native platform using AI.

Using AI to rebuild a platform of that size gave us first-hand experience with AI economics. We employed AI throughout the entire engineering process to write code, review changes, generate tests and accelerate development. It helped us reduce years of engineering to just a few months but also forced us to keep close watch over every single token we consumed and truly consider why we were consuming it.

This experience challenged one of our key assumptions: It turns out that token consumption is influenced as much by architectural decisions as by choice of model.

What token sprawl actually looks like

Indeed, we found that most of the token consumption waste wasn’t due to complex engineering tasks, but the architecture around them; this is something that is referred to as the architecture tax in enterprise AI.

Recursive agents kept spawning subtasks and subagents, and although they technically completed every task, each handoff introduced new prompts and context. Furthermore, frontier reasoning models were being wasted on routine classification tasks that deterministic code could have completed at a fraction of the cost. And, because we hadn’t clearly defined ‘success,’ retry loops continued firing and burning tokens to chase marginal gains, instead of improving business outcomes. Finally, we experienced context inflation, with workflows carrying information from earlier steps long after they had stopped contributing to the decision being made.

None of these decisions seemed expensive in isolation. Things like a few extra prompts, an unnecessary reasoning step or a larger context window barely impacted the cost of a single workflow. Across millions of executions, however, they grew into a level of token consumption that no model upgrade alone could offset.

Designing for token efficiency

Once we figured out where all our tokens were going, we had to determine how to spend them more deliberately.

First, we accepted that not every step in an AI workflow needs the same amount of intelligence. Some tasks legitimately require reasoning, but others are structural, deterministic or repeatable, and are better handled through software, business logic or tools that are reused rather than reasoned through every execution.

Even when a model is required, not all tasks need the same amount of reasoning. This concept is better known as Reasoning Effort Optimization. If you’re designing systems, exploring alternatives or making difficult decisions, high reasoning effort has value. However, once you’ve established the approach, you can usually produce the same outcome with far less reasoning.

It’s comparable to organizations that structure work as a pyramid of expertise. The most experienced engineers tackle the most difficult problems, make important architectural decisions and handle any ambiguity that arises. Then, once their work is complete, they split it into small, well-defined tasks that other engineers and machines can execute consistently.

Allocation is only part of why this works, though; persistence is equally important. A senior engineer’s judgment gets built into interfaces, schemas and conventions, allowing everyone downstream to build on those decisions without having to derive them again. The same applies to AI systems. If you fail to capture their reasoning as a durable artifact like a graph, specification or compiled skill, the system repays for it every single time it runs.

We apply the same principle to AI systems. Advanced reasoning should only be used when judgment is required. Smaller models can handle well-defined implementation work, and deterministic software and reusable tools can execute tasks where the outcome is already known. The goal is to apply the right level of intelligence to each stage of the workflow.

Architect once, inherit everywhere

So, how much of an AI system should teams rebuild for every new workflow?

In our experience, very little. Architectural capabilities like evaluation, orchestration, guardrails, context management and auditability aren’t unique to a single AI application; every enterprise AI system eventually needs them. Rebuilding them for each workflow is a waste of time and money that forces every AI system to solve the same infrastructure problems independently.

It’s much more efficient to move these capabilities into a common harness. Orchestration, governance and evaluation can then be developed, tested and improved at the platform level rather than separately inside every workflow. Each new AI system can reuse this foundation while teams focus on the business logic that makes the application distinct.

This architectural discipline extends to the execution layer. The amount of computation an AI system performs before producing an outcome depends heavily on the context provided, how its instructions are designed and how its agents are structured.

A 2026 study found that consolidating three or four agents into a single call reduced token consumption by 53.7% and latency by 49.5%, with comparable accuracy. Most of these savings came from not repeatedly passing the same context between agents.

The study also demonstrated that, as the number of tasks assigned to each agent increased, the agent became less reliable at choosing the best way to approach each task. However, increased routing helped recover much of that performance. In short, AI efficiency depends on how the work is structured and routed, not just how many agents are involved.

Optimize throughout the lifecycle

Building the right architecture creates the foundation for continuous optimization.

Model selection, for example, shouldn’t be a one-time decision. As models improve and workloads evolve, it’s worth re-evaluating every AI workflow to determine whether the same outcome can be achieved with less reasoning and lower cost. Demonstrating that system design can outweigh raw model capability, Andrew Ng, a computer scientist, AI entrepreneur and Stanford University adjunct professor, highlighted that while zero-shot GPT-3.5 scored 48.1% on the HumanEval coding benchmark and GPT-4 scored 67.0%, wrapping GPT-3.5 in an iterative agentic loop pushed its score to 95.1%.

The same applies to cost visibility. Token economics should be visible across every workflow, model and task so teams can identify ways to reduce costs before they accumulate.

AI is much less expensive than it used to be, but lower costs encourage more use. Organizations can run more workloads and take on more ambitious problems, so it’s even more important to know where the AI is actually creating value.

Allocate intelligence by the value it creates

Most organizations start with fixed token budgets, because they are easy to administer. However, not every AI task has the same value.

Think about AI as an engineering resource, rather than a shared utility. The teams that consistently choose the right model for the right task and avoid unnecessary reasoning should get more compute because their tokens are producing better outcomes.

Over time, I expect enterprises to manage AI the same way they manage any scarce engineering resource — by using it where it has the greatest impact.

item.title: IT reinvention requires mastering the art of translation
item.description:
Today’s most successful IT leaders must be master translators, interpreting technical complexities with clarity and precision for the business units that rely on their services for into decisions and action. Deluxe Chief Technology and Digital Officer Yogaraj “Yogs” Jayaprakasam is among the best at putting this into practice, a strategic imperative he describes as “humanizing” technology.

Rather than beginning with cloud, architecture, or AI, Jayaprakasam frames Deluxe’s IT strategy as one focused on technology “that powers profitable growth.” This translation mastery can also be seen in the five-part series he and CEO Barry McCarthy co-developed to establish a common language around Deluxe’s IT transformation, a sea change that improved not only the way Deluxe does business but the way its customers do as well. And you can see it in how he translates strategy to measurable business, customer, and talent outcomes. Jayaprakasam’s widely read newsletter, “AI Signals: Navigating Change,” is perhaps the clearest expression of his knack for finding the signal and translating it into pragmatic, immediately useful leadership insight.

After a recent episode of the Tech Whisperers podcast, Jayaprakasam and I spent some time discussing why being a master translator is critical for today’s technology leaders and how he separates signal from noise to serve Deluxe’s next reinvention. What follows is that conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Dan Roberts: You’re an engineer by training. When did you realize knowing technology wasn’t enough and that one of your most important jobs was helping others understand what technology makes possible?

Yogs Jayaprakasam: It comes from a pattern I’ve seen throughout my career. As a technologist, you can provide an elegant technology architecture, but the customer wants to know, “If I invest half a million dollars in that, what will I get in return?” I’ve had some of my most high-performing senior technology leaders tell me, “Here are all the great things our team has done,” but they still struggle to figure out, “What does this mean to the company?”

For example, as AI adoption increases, so does exposure to third-party operational risk beyond traditional cybersecurity threats. Recognizing this shift early, my team deployed capabilities such as synthetic monitoring, blast-radius analysis, and proactive service desk operations. The outcome was an 80%+ reduction in system incidents over the last nine months, demonstrating the value of anticipating emerging risks before they impact the business. But when I asked the team what that meant to the business, they couldn’t articulate it.

Technology earns credibility when its impact is expressed in the language of the business — financial performance, risk reduction, customer satisfaction, and employee experience. In this case, I helped the team recast the message as what it truly was: a direct contribution to EBITDA protection and enterprise risk reduction.

I rewrote it as, “It directly protects the EBITDA of the company and reduces our risk posture meaningfully.” Because every time there is an impact, it takes additional time — and costs — for us to fix the problem. That chips away at EBITDA while impacting our customer and employee experience. That’s what the business wants to know.

Deluxe has one of the most inspiring business success stories. Can you talk about where the company started out and where you are today?

Our founder, W.R. Hotchkiss, used the most cutting-edge printing technology of 1915 to introduce uniformity to American bank checks, and he invented what we recognize today as the modern checkbook. Deluxe was a dominant force in paper payments and used that trusted history and massive business network to move with the times. Today, we are a digital payments and data company offering merchant services solutions that provide credit card processing, payment settlement enablement, the payment gateway, and data-driven marketing solutions for B2B businesses, financial institutions, and various industries.

When this business transformation journey started, we were around 30% payments and data. As of this past quarter, we were at 52% payments and data, and we are potentially trending towards 60% payments and data with the recent acquisition of Celero Commerce. So we are a payments and data company with the legacy checks division still being profitable, supporting our cash flow and business growth.

You’ve described Deluxe’s journey as one of reinvention, not simply transformation. Why is that distinction important?

Typically, people use modern technology to do the same thing they were doing before. It could be a manufacturing company that still does the same manufacturing, but now you are applying a digital order management system to accelerate fulfillment. At legacy Deluxe, the product we were building was checks, so we identified ourselves as a manufacturing company. Adopting digital technology for that process simply enabled it to be more efficient. That’s transformation.

But the job customers trusted us to do for more than 100 years has largely moved to credit cards, digital payments, embedded payments — all things that no longer require manufacturing. Now, technology is how we build those services and deliver. The mission is the same — to make sure the payments transactions are safely and quickly completed — but we had to reinvent what we do, how we do it, and the whole mindset of delivering a software-driven product.

Every function inside the company had to change. Finance had to change the way we do revenue recognition. In manufacturing, you have to think about inventory management to optimize your balance sheet. It’s totally different on the payments side. The talent is different. The sales talent is different — somebody who used to sell a tangible product versus somebody who is selling a service level and functionalities. The tech stack is different. For the technology function, this means you have to build applications and platforms that are always on to facilitate those digital payments and data solutions. Every part is evolving in every sense to make the whole bigger than its parts. That’s why it is a reinvention story, not just a transformation story.

How do you translate your technology strategy into something everyone, from the boardroom to an engineer at the keyboard, can understand and act on?

I have a one-page strategy slide that begins with “Technology’s mission inside Deluxe is to power profitable growth.” This was co-created with my CEO and the rest of the executive leadership team. We connected that to five strategic pillars:

First is Deliver Measurable Business Value. That means aligning technology investment to growth. This an executive leadership team and board pillar — it is of special interest to the leaders responsible for investment decisions — but my team will experience it through the projects we invest in.

The second pillar is Build Modern Products and Platforms. That is where the investment turns into initiatives. Can the core platforms we are building be reused in many business units? We identified data, AI, and APIs as a core part of our platform strategy to drive reuse and leverage. For example, if I built an API that can extract invoice solutions, every business that needs an invoice solution can consume it.

Third is Scale AI Responsibly. This is about using AI with our data to drive more automation efficiency for the internal functions. We used AI to eliminate a 50-year-old mainframe and move to the cloud. We are using AI to continue to drive resiliency on that platform but also to improve our legacy unit, because, according to the Federal Reserve, 60% to 80% of businesses still use the check product, and many of those businesses are banks, even our largest banks.

Number four is Strengthen Cyber Resilience and Trust, where we continue to innovate in not only cybersecurity but also systems availability, proactive resiliency, all those things to protect our revenue, EBITDA, and our existing business.

The fifth pillar is Grow Next-Generation Talent and Culture, which is investing in our people across the company, giving them the right tools and AI skills in an accountable, collaborative culture.

Stepping back, the first pillar talks about strategic investment through the lens of the ELT and board. But the next three pillars talk about technology’s job: driving profitable growth and improving the margin. Products and the platform contribute to driving the growth. AI usage contributes to expanding the margin. The trust and governance comes from next-gen cyber resiliency. Then we’re investing in and training our people.

You’ve told me the CEO and executive leadership team are your “first team.” How has being on that team and serving on boards, changed the way you think and lead?

Becoming part of the executive leadership team is your best opportunity to truly become a business leader, not just a technology leader. Your first duty is to the team that you are a part of, which is the ELT. But serving on boards gives another dimension for a technology leader. How you think and act in the executive leadership team is different from being on the governance team of a board. How you observe and guide operating teams is different.

It makes you realize that you are not going to play the same role on every team. For my function, I am the head of technology. For my ELT, I’m one of the teammates who makes a decision come to life. As part of a board, my job is to help assess as a group if the operating team is representing the right outcomes for the shareholders that you represent as well.

These are, in my opinion, the best opportunities to evolve to be a fully rounded leader. Business is the ultimate team sport. Individual excellence is valuable, but collective excellence is what creates lasting impact. I believe the hallmark of a successful technology leader is the ability to seamlessly shift between leading and serving, always doing what best advances the success of the team and the enterprise.

There’s no shortage of AI content. What did you believe was missing when you created your newsletter, “AI Signals: Navigating Change,” and how are you using it to help audiences separate signal from noise?

It began when ChatGPT was released in November 2022. I observed many of my peers trying to figure out how to bring ChatGPT into their organizations and how to drive value with it. Then, many AI companies started coming out. Many models started coming out. It was extremely hard for any company to decide what to do with the technology.

That triggered me to research and review the last 70 years of technology evolution. I wanted to understand, when a moment like this happens, whether it is through the internet, web development, mobile, or big data and machine learning, what occurs afterward that becomes durable, and what lessons can we learn from those moments?

What quickly became clear is, all of those changed how you solve a problem inside your business, not what you need to change. Eighty percent of what you do inside every business is the same. We are a 112-year-old company; 80% of what we do is the same. Go through every department — we all have to do the same things, but we have to do it faster, better, and cheaper.

So instead of chasing what is changing, I tried to go back to what is not changing in this chaotic moment. Then I thought, how can I draw attention to those things that are not changing? That’s how “AI Signals” was born. I realized that I need to write about it so that it is clear in my head. The newsletter provides a forum for input and collaboration with industry peers so we know how to make the right decisions for our organizations.

What signals are you paying closest attention to right now, and how are they shaping what you’re preparing Deluxe for next? How do you know when it’s time to change your mind?

I track what’s happening because of AI through three lenses: One, because Deluxe is all about payments and data, I keenly watch what’s happening in the payments industry, paying close attention to agentic commerce and how much it will pick up steam, and how much trust humans are placing in agents to make decisions on their behalf to make purchases, and things like that.

The second is a continuous focus on cybersecurity. As AI continues to mature, that space will continue to expose what we took for granted in the past, where we’ve said some vulnerabilities are medium and low, you can get exceptions that linger, and also how you handle the end of life for a technology. All those things are dramatically changing, because several low vulnerabilities chained together by an AI tool could become a path for malevolent AI to penetrate. And that doesn’t even include the threat posed by well-intended frontier models like those made by OpenAI, which accidentally penetrated a government database last week. The focus is on vigilance about patterns of AI behavior and how to effectively defend our companies.

The third lens is much more personal to me but also relevant to my job, which is how we view AI’s impact on talent. It is already redefining our jobs, and the biggest work in front of us is legal, compliance, HR, and technology partnering together to really figure out how to retrain our talent to use AI to stay relevant for the jobs we need to deliver. Whether you apply your lens as a leader or you have broader community concerns, we all have to contribute to the talent adjustments.

I don’t just rely on my opinions and my own research. I talk to real people at every level, and if my research does not fit well, is not practical, or is a couple of steps ahead of where the reality is, I rein it in and go from there. I have about a dozen volunteers for “AI Signals” who meet with me every Sunday, and we go through the ideas before I post. And there are articles that they’ve brought their own real examples to. Those people come from different industries and different backgrounds, so I’m pressure testing in those areas as well.

Perhaps the biggest lesson in Jayaprakasam’s approach to being a master translator is that it starts with being a master learner. He is equally intentional about staying current to develop an informed point of view as he is in challenging his own thinking, engaging peers with different perspectives, and changing course when the signals suggest he should. With virtually every company confronting reinvention in the AI era, the best leaders will need to strike that same balance, while still having the courage to move.

For more insights from Yogaraj Jayaprakasam’s leadership playbook, tune in to the Tech Whisperers.
