item.title: What hundreds of Microsoft 365 deployments have taught me about cybersecurity
item.description:
I’ve spent more than 20 years running IT and security for organizations across California and around the country. Over that time, my team has taken over, deployed and cleaned up Microsoft 365 environments for law firms, commercial real estate companies, manufacturers, healthcare practices and schools. We’ve supported more than 7,500 users along the way.

After working with that many tenants, the biggest takeaway is simple: most Microsoft 365 security problems aren’t especially sophisticated. Usually, a control was never turned on, only covered part of the organization, or somebody made an exception years ago to keep something working and it was never revisited. Microsoft gives organizations a lot to work with. More often than not, the problem is how the environment was configured and maintained, not a lack of security tools.

These are the issues we run into most often and the areas I’d look at first.

Most environments are still running on their original settings

When we first assess a tenant, we often find that nobody has really gone back through the security settings since it was originally set up. MFA may cover some users but not everybody. Legacy authentication is still allowed. There are too many global administrators. Nobody is quite sure when audit logging was last reviewed.

Last year we took over a 45-person medical practice that had been on Microsoft 365 for almost a decade. We found nine global administrator accounts, including two belonging to employees who had left years earlier. MFA was enabled, but only for the physicians. The front desk and billing staff, who handled the most patient data, had none.

Usually, nobody intentionally ignored security. The company grew, email kept working, people got busy and the original setup stayed in place. We see this constantly. Something working every day doesn’t necessarily mean it is configured the way you would want it configured today.

For a smaller organization without dedicated identity management, Microsoft’s security defaults are a good place to start. They require MFA and block legacy authentication without adding another license. As the environment gets more complex, and assuming the licensing supports it, conditional access gives you much more control over who can sign in, from where and from what device.

MFA is the starting point, not the finish line

At this point, most business leaders know MFA needs to be enabled. What still gets missed is the idea that turning it on somehow finishes the job.

Attackers have adjusted to MFA. Push fatigue attacks still work because eventually somebody may approve a prompt just to make it stop. Adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits can steal a live session token and get around standard MFA altogether. OAuth consent phishing is another issue: a user can be tricked into approving a malicious application through what looks like a legitimate Microsoft or Google consent screen. At that point, changing the user’s password may not even remove the access.

A few months ago, a paralegal at a law firm we support clicked what looked like a shared document from opposing counsel and signed in through a convincing Microsoft login page. She had MFA and completed the prompt, but the page was relaying her session in real time. Within minutes the attacker was in her mailbox from overseas. We caught it through an impossible-travel alert, revoked the session and reset the account before any client data left.

There are a handful of things we normally tighten up here. Use number matching in the authenticator app. Put administrators and other high-risk users on phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 keys or passkeys. Don’t let users approve any third-party application they want. And where licensing allows it, use conditional access so a password or stolen session by itself isn’t enough to get into the environment.

Legacy authentication remains the open side door

This one still surprises a lot of executives. They know MFA is enabled and assume that means every sign-in is protected. That isn’t always the case. Legacy protocols such as POP, IMAP and older SMTP connections don’t support MFA, which can leave a path around the control.

Microsoft has retired a lot of legacy authentication already, but we still come across exceptions that were left in place for an old scanner, a line-of-business application or sometimes one user’s device. Find out what actually still needs it, fix or replace that dependency, and close the exception. We have seen organizations leave a security hole open for years because of one multifunction printer.

Licensing determines what security is actually available

Licensing is another area that causes a surprising amount of confusion. Two plans can sound almost identical while giving the IT team very different security capabilities. Office 365 E3 and Microsoft 365 E3 are a good example: Microsoft 365 E3 includes Intune device management and Entra ID P1 conditional access, while Office 365 E3 does not.

We once had a healthcare client with a departing employee who kept a company laptop with patient records on it. Leadership assumed we could lock or wipe it remotely. We couldn’t. They were licensed for Office 365 E3, not Microsoft 365 E3, so the device had never been enrolled in Intune. We got the laptop back, but only after several uncomfortable days, and they upgraded their licensing the following week.

So before putting together a security roadmap, I would first confirm exactly what licenses are in place and what those licenses actually include. We’ve had more than one situation where leadership assumed a security capability was available simply because the Microsoft plan name sounded similar.

Email is still where most incidents begin

For us, email is still where a large percentage of incidents start. It may be a credential phishing page, a malicious link, or an inbox rule created after somebody has already gained access to the account.

Business email compromise is especially dangerous because the attacker often doesn’t do anything obvious right away. They get into a mailbox, create forwarding rules or hide replies, and wait. The goal may simply be to sit there until an invoice or wire transfer gives them an opportunity. According to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, reported cybercrime losses reached $16.6 billion in 2024, and BEC continues to be one of the more expensive categories of fraud.

At one law firm, an attacker compromised a mailbox and created a rule that quietly moved any email containing “invoice” or “wire” into an unused folder. Two weeks later, a client received updated wiring instructions for a settlement payment from what looked like the firm’s own account. The client called to confirm before sending the funds, and that phone call is the only reason the money didn’t go out.

We normally put several controls around this. Block automatic forwarding to outside domains. Alert when inbox rules are created or changed. Most importantly, have an internal policy that any change to payment or wiring instructions gets confirmed verbally using a phone number you already know. That last one has nothing to do with cybersecurity software, but it can stop a very expensive mistake.

Privileged accounts need their own standard

The global administrator list should be short, intentional and documented. We also don’t want somebody using the same privileged account to read email and browse the web all day. It sounds basic, but we correct this all the time.

Use separate administrative accounts, put phishing-resistant MFA on them, and use just-in-time elevation where the licensing supports it. A compromised global administrator account gives an attacker an enormous amount of control, so we treat those accounts differently from a normal user.

Logging only helps if it’s configured before you need it

When something does happen, we immediately need to know what happened, when it started and what the attacker touched. If the right logging wasn’t enabled beforehand, or the retention period is too short, sometimes you simply can’t reconstruct the whole incident after the fact.

I’d much rather configure logging on day one and never use it than reconstruct an incident from partial data. CISA’s Secure Cloud Business Applications (SCuBA) baselines are an excellent, free reference for which settings to enable and how to verify them.

Where I would start

Microsoft 365 can be a very secure platform. In most environments we take over, the issue isn’t that Microsoft was missing some critical security feature. It’s usually a relatively short list of settings, permissions and exceptions that accumulated over time.

If I were reviewing an environment this quarter, these are the four things I would verify first:

  1. Administrative access is minimal and protected with phishing-resistant MFA.
  2. Legacy authentication is blocked.
  3. MFA covers every user, and users can’t approve third-party apps unchecked.
  4. You would have complete logs if something happened tomorrow.

Those four checks won’t solve every security problem, but they eliminate a lot of the issues we repeatedly find when we’re brought in to assess an environment or clean up after an incident.

item.title: Workday expands AI ambitions with C1.ai identity platform acquisition
item.description:
Fresh off its $1.1 billion acquisition of AI startup Sana, Workday is making another bet on enterprise AI, this time targeting the governance challenge. The company said it will acquire agentic identity platform C1.ai to help customers manage and secure AI agents operating across enterprise applications.

The acquisition will build on Workday’s Agent System of Record, which gives enterprises a centralized view of their AI agents, by adding controls over what those agents can access across Workday and other enterprise systems, the company said.

That would allow enterprises to grant agents the permissions they need to perform specific tasks and revoke them when those tasks are completed, rather than risk agents retaining access to data and applications they no longer need, it added.

The combined capabilities could also help streamline access management for employees as they join an organization, change roles, or leave, reducing the manual work involved in managing permissions while limiting potential security gaps, it further said.

These governance and identity management capabilities become increasingly important as Workday, alongside the acquisition, also continues to expand the role of AI agents across its suite.

During the week, the company announced several updates to Sana, including making it the new home interface for its applications.

The interface brings tasks, decisions, meetings, and agent activity into one place, allowing employees to use natural-language prompts to get Workday agents to complete tasks rather than simply retrieve information, the company said.

The company also extended Sana into third-party tools, including Microsoft Teams, Slack, and Microsoft Copilot, allowing employees to invoke Workday capabilities from the applications they already use.

That expanded ability to invoke Workday agents across applications underscores the need for enterprises to govern what these agents can access and do across systems. C1.ai’s acquisition is expected to close by the end of January.

item.title: MCP is changing the questions marketers can afford to ask
item.description:
Picture a regional marketing director on a Monday morning. She’s got 80 locations, a cup of coffee, and a nagging feeling that something is off in the Southeast. Reviews seem quieter. A couple of stores got new managers last month. Are those two things related?

Not long ago, finding out meant pulling an export, building a pivot table, pulling a second export from another system, and stitching it all together in a spreadsheet. Or, more realistically, filing a request with an analyst and waiting. Most weeks, the question simply never got asked.

Now she types it into the AI assistant her company already rolled out, and it answers using live data from the systems where that data actually lives.

The technology making that possible is the Model Context Protocol, or MCP. You’ve probably read plenty of “what is MCP” explainers by now, so I won’t add another. Instead, I want to talk about what changes for marketing teams, especially those managing lots of locations, when a cross-system question gets this cheap to ask. And what CIOs need to get right before it becomes the normal way marketing works.

The real shift: the join moves into the conversation

Here’s the short version of how MCP works. Your AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, or something your team built) is the host. Each business system, like your reputation platform, ad account, or CRM, publishes an MCP server. That server tells the assistant, in plain language, what it can do: “I can summarize reviews for a group of locations,” or “I can check whether your listings match across Google and Apple Maps.” The assistant reads that menu, picks the right tools for the question, and calls them.

That’s really it. But two things fall out of it that matter a lot for marketing.

First, the integration math gets much friendlier. Connecting four assistants to ten marketing systems used to mean up to 40 custom integrations. With a shared protocol, each assistant learns MCP once, and each system publishes one server. The conversation shifts from “should we build this integration?” to “which servers do we approve?”

Second, and this is the one people underestimate, the join moves. In a traditional stack, combining review data with POS and CRM data happens in a warehouse, on a schedule, through a pipeline someone has to own. With MCP, a regional leader can connect three systems to the same assistant and ask one question across all of them. The model does the join on the spot, right in the conversation, using that person’s own permissions.

That doesn’t replace your data warehouse. What it does is make a long tail of one-off, “I just want to know” questions affordable for the first time. In multi-location marketing, that long tail is where a lot of the useful insight lives.

It’s also not a science project anymore. Anthropic donated MCP to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation last December, with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and AWS all involved. And the July 2026 spec update made it far more enterprise friendly. It now scales on ordinary infrastructure, lets IT control which tools can run at the gateway, and gives tools a standard way to stop and ask a human, “Are you sure?” before doing anything.

Location marketing is the ultimate stress test

If MCP works for brick-and-mortar marketing, it’ll work almost anywhere. Do the math on a mid-sized brand. Three hundred locations, each listed on Google, Apple Maps, Bing, and Yelp, add up to 1,200 profiles that all need the same name, address, phone number, and hours. Every location collects reviews every week on multiple sites. And each one sits inside a hierarchy of district, region, brand, and maybe franchisee, where every level is supposed to see a different slice.

On top of that, the questions people ask are almost always comparative. Nobody asks, “What’s store 114’s rating?” They ask, “Which stores in the Southeast are slipping, and why?” Those are exactly the questions dashboards handle badly, and exports handle slowly.

My colleague Kristi Melani recently wrote here about how reputation data is now moving in two directions: outward to the AI engines customers use, and inward to the assistants your own teams use. MCP is the plumbing for that inward direction, and it raises the stakes on data quality on both sides. A wrong Sunday hour on Apple Maps used to mislead one customer. Now it can mislead that customer’s AI and your CMO’s AI at the same time. Customers already punish that mistake: Rio SEO found that 53% of consumers are unlikely to visit a business with incorrect listings.

What this actually looks like

The pattern I’m seeing in multi-location brands is pretty consistent. MCP doesn’t replace the reputation platform, the listings tool, or the ad account. It changes who gets to ask them questions, how often, and in what combinations. A few examples:

  • The field leader asks, “Which of my locations collected zero reviews this month, and what happened to their scores?” That used to be a weekly export, filtered by hand.
  • The local search lead asks, “Where do our hours or phone numbers disagree across Google, Apple Maps, Bing, and Yelp badly enough that an AI assistant would get them wrong?” That used to be a quarterly audit.
  • The paid media lead asks, “Which markets are we spending the most in where our average rating dropped below 4.0?” Google already publishes an official Google Ads MCP server, so that’s now one question instead of two dashboards and a spreadsheet.
  • The CMO asks for the first-half reputation readout by market, with the three biggest opportunities. That used to be two or three days of deck-building.

The industry-specific versions get even more interesting. A dealer group can read service department reviews next to repair order data. A property manager can line up resident complaints with open maintenance tickets, building by building. A restaurant brand can check whether a spike in “cold food” reviews lines up with a change in delivery partners. None of that needed new infrastructure. It just needed both systems to have a server, and the person asking to have access to both.

Tool design matters more than tool count

Here’s something that surprises a lot of teams once they start piloting: the shape of the tools matters more than how many there are.

An AI assistant works within a limited context window and a limited number of tool calls. If a regional director asks about 300 locations and the server only offers a one-location-at-a-time lookup, the model has to make 300 calls and juggle 300 results. It’ll be slow, it’ll be expensive, or it’ll quietly skip some. A server that can roll up an entire region in one call hands the model a small, tidy result it can actually reason about.

The same goes for definitions. If “sentiment” is calculated differently on every review site, the model will happily compare numbers that aren’t comparable. MCP can’t fix that, because it just moves data. Consistent metrics have to exist before the assistant ever sees them.

So when you evaluate a marketing MCP server, don’t ask how many tools it has. Ask whether it can answer a portfolio-level question in one or two calls, using metrics that mean the same thing everywhere.

Connecting is easy. Governing is the real work.

Hooking an assistant up to a marketing system now takes minutes. Deciding whether you should is where CIOs and AI governance teams are spending their time. Four questions come up in nearly every conversation I have.

Whose permissions does the assistant use? The safest setup is for each person to sign in as themselves, so the assistant inherits their existing access. A district manager who sees 12 locations in the platform should see 12 through the assistant, not 300. What you want to avoid is a shared API key baked into a connector, which quietly gives everyone the widest access anyone has.

Can it change anything? Reading a review summary and posting a public reply to a customer are very different levels of risk. Review responses and listing fixes are where AI promises the biggest time savings, but they’re also public and attached to your brand. Plenty of organizations are starting read-only and adding write access one tool at a time, with a human approving each action.

What is the assistant actually reading? This one is specific to reputation data, and it doesn’t get talked about enough. Reviews are written by the public. A review can include text aimed at an AI rather than a person, essentially an instruction hiding in plain sight. If the same conversation also has tools that can send email or edit records, that’s a real risk. Keeping reputation access read-only, and keeping anything that publishes behind a confirmation step, shrinks that exposure a lot.

Where does the data go? Review text can contain names, health details, and other personal information. In healthcare, a review can effectively confirm that someone is a patient. Governance teams need to know which AI tools are approved for which kinds of data, and what each AI vendor’s enterprise agreement says about retention and training.

Underneath all four is a simpler truth: MCP makes your data easier to reach. It doesn’t make it more accurate. Gartner predicts that through 2026, organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. For local marketing, “AI-ready” means one location list every system agrees on, consistent metrics, and listings that are actually correct. If your store IDs don’t match between the reputation platform, the POS, and the CRM, the assistant’s answers will break in exactly the spots an analyst used to patch by hand.

Where to start

The organizations moving fastest treat MCP as a joint project between IT and marketing, not a feature marketing flips on by itself. Here’s the path I’d recommend:

  1. Start with the questions, not the systems. Ask your regional leaders for the ten questions they ask most and wait longest to get answered. That tells you which servers actually matter.
  2. Go read-only, per user, in one region. Approve a small set of servers that inherit existing permissions, and pilot with a team that’s already using an enterprise AI assistant.
  3. Clean up your location list before you scale. It’s unglamorous work. It’s also what decides whether cross-system answers are right.
  4. Add write access slowly, with a human in the loop. Review responses and listing corrections is the obvious next step. Set your brand voice and compliance rules before the first reply goes out.

Whatever servers you evaluate, make sure they work across every major assistant. An open standard is what saves you from rebuilding everything the next time your company switches AI vendors.

From questions to agents

Right now, most marketing use of MCP is a person asking a question. The next phase is software asking on a schedule: an agent that checks every location each morning, flags a listing that’s drifted, or drafts replies to overnight reviews for a manager to approve. Those agents will run on the same servers answering human questions today.

It’s already happening in other parts of the business. When the latest MCP spec was announced, Honeycomb shared that nearly 20% of its monthly interactive queries now come from agents, not people. Marketing data won’t be far behind.

That’s why the choices made in this first wave matter so much. When we built the Reputation MCP Server, we made it read-only and permission-based from day one, because an agent is only as trustworthy as the data it can reach and the access it’s allowed.

The protocol is open to everyone. What will set brands apart is the quality of the data they plug into it and how carefully they govern it. For marketers responsible for hundreds of storefronts, the questions that used to wait for the quarterly review are about to get asked every Monday morning. The brands that get their data ready will see their locations more clearly than ever.

For more information, visit reputation.com.

About the author

Reputation

Kristi Melani is a transformational marketing executive with 30+ years of experience building high-performing teams, scalable marketing operations, and revenue-driving programs across high-growth startups and billion-dollar global enterprises. As CMO of Reputation, she leads global marketing strategy with a focus on brand trust, go-to-market excellence, and customer-centric growth.

Kristi is known for building marketing organizations from the ground up—creating clear processes, measurable frameworks, and cultures rooted in accountability, transparency, and performance. Prior to Reputation, she served as Chief Marketing Officer at Telesign and held senior marketing leadership roles at Anaplan, Poly, and Plantronics, where she led global teams, drove significant pipeline growth, and supported large-scale transformations and integrations.

item.title: Human in the loop is an engineering problem
item.description:
A customer leaves a one-star review at one of your locations. An AI drafts a reply in seconds. It’s warm, on-brand, grammatically perfect, and it thanks the customer for their feedback and invites them back soon.

The review was about a customer who slipped and was hurt in the parking lot.

Nothing in that reply is factually false. It would pass a spell-checker, a brand-voice check, and probably a quick skim from a busy manager. It’s still the wrong answer, and if it goes out publicly, it’s the kind of wrong that ends up in a screenshot.

I spend most of my time building systems that put AI to work on reputation data: reviews, listings, surveys, and the replies and summaries generated from them. The most important lesson I’ve learned is that “human in the loop” is an engineering problem. Where the human sits, what they see, what gets routed to them and what doesn’t—all of that is system design.

Get it right, and AI can move fast without embarrassing you. Get it wrong, and you either drown your reviewers or give them a rubber stamp.

What “human in the loop” means

The phrase gets used loosely, so let’s pin it down. From a systems perspective, there are three oversight modes:

  • Human in the loop is a synchronous approval gate. The AI proposes, a person approves, and nothing happens until they do.
  • Human on the loop is asynchronous monitoring. The AI acts on its own, while people watch dashboards, review samples, and get alerts, and they can step in or shut it off.
  • Human out of the loop is full automation. Guardrails and logging only, no person in the path.

The mistake I see most often is choosing one mode for an entire product. Choose it per action instead. Pulling a summary of last month’s reviews and publishing a reply to a customer can live in the same application, but they carry completely different risk profiles and shouldn’t share an oversight mode. A good system might run a dozen actions out of the loop, a handful on the loop, and gate one or two behind a person.

Regulators are writing the same principle into law. The EU AI Act’s Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed so people can effectively oversee them, with oversight “commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use,” and it specifically calls out the danger of people over-relying on AI output. Most marketing uses won’t fall into the Act’s high-risk categories, but Article 14 shows where expectations are heading.

The U.S. military’s directive on autonomy in weapon systems has asked for “appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force” since 2012. That means the appropriate level of judgment for the stakes rather than a human on every decision, which is the same principle at far higher stakes.

Accurate isn’t the same as right

Large language models generate the most plausible next words, and they don’t look facts up unless you build the LLMs to persistently fact-check or cite claims. When plausible and true diverge, you get a hallucination, a confident, fluent answer that’s made up. The fluency is the dangerous part, because it reads exactly like a correct answer.

When we test AI output, we check for two kinds of accuracy.

Factual accuracy asks whether a statement is true. Did a location page list a service that location doesn’t offer? These errors are easier to catch, because you can compare them against a source of truth.

Contextual accuracy asks whether it’s true here, now, for this person. These errors are sneakier, because every individual fact can check out:

  • The holiday hours are correct, but they’re the hours for a different region.
  • A sentiment model scores “great, another two-hour wait” as positive, because it reads the word “great” and misses the sarcasm.
  • And our injury review reply from the top of this piece: right tone for 95% of reviews, wrong for this one.

Not every error carries the same weight, and your system should know the difference. I think about it in three tiers:

  • Embarrassing: a fabricated statistic in a published report, or an off-key public reply. Painful, fixable, and memorable for the wrong reasons.
  • Foundational: an error early in a project that everything else gets built on, like a quarter’s worth of misclassified review themes feeding a campaign strategy that’s wrong from the start.
  • Dangerous: errors that can hurt people. In marketing, that’s a healthcare review reply that confirms someone is a patient, or wrong pharmacy hours during a storm. Outside marketing, it’s AI in public safety, healthcare, infrastructure, and defense, where “mostly right” is not an acceptable standard and human judgment isn’t optional.

The tiers matter because they decide where the human goes. You can’t afford a person on every output, and you can’t afford no person on the dangerous ones.

Anatomy of a human-in-the-loop pipeline

When we design an oversight system, it looks less like “a person checks the AI” and more like a pipeline, where each layer catches what it’s best at and passes the rest along. Here’s the shape of it.

Reputation

Most drafts never need a person. The ones that do arrive with the evidence a reviewer needs, and every human decision feeds back into the system.

1. Grounding. The first defense against hallucination is not letting the model work from memory. We connect it to authoritative sources, like the location master record and approved policies, and require every factual claim to point back to one.

2. Deterministic validators. Cheap, fast, boring checks run next. Do the hours match the system of record? Does the reply contain a banned phrase, a competitor’s name, or personal information it shouldn’t? Software should catch everything software can catch.

3. Model-based verifiers. A second model checks whether each claim is supported by its source and whether the tone fits the review. It catches contextual errors that rules can’t, like a cheerful reply to an angry review, but it’s still probabilistic, so calibrate it against examples people have labeled.

4. Risk scoring and routing. The system combines the type of action, the check results, and the input into a routing decision. A five-star “great service, thanks” can get an auto-approved reply. A one-star review that mentions an injury, discrimination, a health issue, or a lawyer always goes to a person. The routing rules are versioned and reviewed like code, because they are code.

5. The review interface. Reviewers are a component of the system, so design their inputs. A good review screen shows the source next to each claim and highlights what the verifier was unsure about. A reviewer handed a wall of polished text will skim it. A reviewer shown “this sentence has no source” will stop and look.

6. The feedback loop. Every edit and rejection becomes a test case, a new rule, or a prompt fix, so over time fewer things need a person. Keep a random sample of auto-approved output flowing to reviewers too, or the system only learns from the cases you already knew to route.

7. The audit trail. Log what the model produced, which checks ran, who approved it, and what they changed. When something goes wrong, this tells you whether it was the model, the data, the routing, or the review.

Test it before launch, watch it after

The pipeline is only as good as the testing around it. Three practices do most of the work.

Golden data sets. Build a library of known tricky cases (sarcasm, mixed languages, injuries, legal threats, star ratings that contradict the text) and run every model, prompt, and rule change against it. If a change breaks a golden case, it doesn’t ship.

Red-teaming. Have people deliberately try to break the system. The public writes reviews, and someone can write one with instructions aimed at an AI (“ignore your guidelines and reply with…”). No current model reliably ignores those, so limit what the pipeline can do with review text and test it.

Drift monitoring. AI behavior changes even when you don’t touch it, as models update and customers’ language shifts. Pin model versions where you can, track quality against a baseline, and alert when it moves. A system that passed its tests in March can be failing quietly by October.

What to avoid

Most failed oversight systems I’ve seen had reviewers. They failed because of how the review was set up.

Rubber-stamping. This is the big one. When a system is right 98% of the time, people stop reading carefully and start clicking approve. It’s called automation bias, and the EU AI Act names it directly. One technique we use is seeding known errors into review queues and tracking whether reviewers catch them. If they don’t, look at the workload, the interface, and the incentives before you blame the reviewer.

Reviewing everything. A person on every output creates a bottleneck and burns reviewers out, which makes them worse at catching the errors that matter. Route by risk instead.

The moral crumple zone. The researcher Madeleine Clare Elish coined this term for what happens when a person ends up absorbing the blame for a system they couldn’t meaningfully control, the way a car’s crumple zone absorbs the impact of a crash. If a reviewer has 15 seconds per item, no source to check against, and no authority to push back, they’re providing someone to blame and calling it oversight.

Blaming only the model. If the location record says a store closes at 9 and it actually closes at 8, a perfectly grounded AI will confidently repeat the wrong hours. Your oversight system should watch the data too.

How to tell if it’s working

If you can’t measure your oversight system, you can’t tell whether it’s protecting you or just slowing you down. Three numbers matter most:

  • Escape rate. How many errors were found after publishing, by a customer, a manager, or an audit? This is the number that tells you whether the whole pipeline works.
  • Seeded-error catch rate. Of the known errors you planted in review queues, what share did reviewers catch? This is your direct measure of rubber-stamping.
  • Routing accuracy. Of the items sent to people, how many needed a person? Of the items auto-approved, how many should have been reviewed?

The check I trust most is simpler. If your reviewers almost never change anything, find out why. Either the AI really is that good on that type of content, in which case you can loosen the routing and save everyone time, or nobody’s really reading. You need to know which one it is.

Where this is headed

So far, most of this has been about reviewing what AI says. The next phase is about governing what AI does. As agents start taking actions on their own, such as updating listings, posting replies, or opening tickets, oversight shifts from approving individual outputs to setting boundaries: what an agent is allowed to do on its own, what it must stop and ask about, and what it can never do.

The standards are starting to build this in. The Model Context Protocol specification, the open standard many AI assistants now use to connect to business systems, says there should always be a human in the loop who can deny a tool call, and recommends that apps ask the user to confirm sensitive operations. Where that gate sits is still each app’s design decision.

The human role is changing too. Less proofreading of every output, more supervising: writing the routing rules, handling the exceptions the system escalates, auditing samples, and deciding where the boundaries should sit. At Reputation, that’s how we think about the people in our loops. Their job is to teach the system what “right” looks like.

As models get better, the errors that slip through get rarer and subtler, which makes them harder to spot. A system that’s wrong 10% of the time keeps everyone alert. A system that’s wrong 0.5% of the time lulls people into trusting it, and that’s when a well-designed loop matters most.
